utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtrooms. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. And may I inform the Registrar that my LiveNote is not working. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and David Martini are presenting Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is anything that we need do before we go into closed session in order to deal with the -- to complete the application that is before us?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the application I have, which I hope Your Honours have been informed about, I've told the Defence, is to ask for a little more time this morning, once have you dealt with the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we've been alerted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that I may -- if he's sworn in, just for those purposes, so that I may have leave still to speak to him. I'm going to ask for, once we've dealt with protective measures, if we go -- take the rest of the session so that I can speak to him about the matters he was asked to check overnight and inform the Defence so they have time to take instructions. I don't think for one moment this witness will require the whole of the rest of this week. As I understand it, there is unlikely to be any cross-examination on behalf of Mr. Zupljanin. I've asked -- we've asked for four hours. It's taking my life in my hands, but I doubt that it will take four hours. And so even with the delay, we should complete the witness by Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, before we do that, is -- are Your Honours intending to ask the normal questions? Because, if so, we ought to be in private session. About this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is the witness's profession a problem, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mean, if you're going to ask him ethnicity, profession, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour is quite right. Obviously his profession is going to come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it just depends on how many personal details Your Honours intend to ask for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on the screen 10236.12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a map of Sarajevo and the surrounding municipalities which shows the -- the main ethnicity of the various towns and municipalities. As we can see, Pale is shown as majority Serb. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I mean -- in -- I don't know whether to go --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we better go back into private session, I suppose, Your Honours. It's quite difficult, this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we proceed, I'll share with you what the Chamber is just discussing; that is, that inasmuch as the last exhibit was tendered to establish the question which you didn't realise at the time was an adjudicated fact, whether it was strictly necessary to do so. But we think that no harm is done but that it is a consideration you will bear in mind for the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the reason we've been producing all these maps, even though we've got adjudicated facts, is, although we all say the majority is Serb in the adjudicated fact, as indeed, I think, for most municipalities, it is going to become important in, I think, all municipalities that some of the areas had Muslim villages or the like, and that is shown on these maps which doesn't appear from the adjudicated fact. So that's at reason I'm asking for each of these maps. And, indeed, it's one of the things that has gone to the back of our minds. But, Your Honours, we will provide, as I say, a booklet of all of these maps for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have up, please, on the screens, 65 ter 3419.30. It needs to be turned the other way around. Yup. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you indicate - and you're able to draw on the screen - the SJB in Pale? The usher will give you -- oh, you've got something there. No, maybe the usher is going give you a pen. Just indicate it with an arrow. The usher will give you a pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's this building here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... sorry, sir. You -- have you marked anything? I don't think you have. I don't think you've been given a pen to mark. I'm told you can't mark it because we have a defective pen. All right. Perhaps I can deal with it this way. We can see in the middle of the picture a building with a red roof, a very bright red roof. These photographs were taken last year. Can you tell us what the building with the bright red roof is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's here, where you can see some kind of opening in the middle of the building. In front of it we can see a building with a blue roof. I think -- that's a bakery. At least it was during the war. And then under that we see residential building. So, yes, that's the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There's some confusion. I think you're indicating and will do when you get the working pen that it's the building behind the red -- the really bright red roof building, the one where we can see with a hole in the middle of it - a gap in the middle of it, as opposed to a hole - is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to know or remember what the building -- buildings with the really disgustingly bright red roof is? [Microphone not activated] ... if not, don't guess.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry. That's all I want.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's fairly clear, even though it's not marked, what he's indicating is the SJB. So could I ask that that photograph be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1450, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the next document, can I ask that it not go up on the screen for -- for the public. It's document 0 -- 65 ter 2449. And it's at tab 53 of the documents. And there's an English translation. Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is that a plan that you -- that you prepared of the Pale Police Station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can't see the -- we need to -- if we could have the second page -- well, it's all on one page on mine, but we only seem to have part of the English translation. Go -- yeah, go to the -- no, I don't know what you're showing there. No. It should have numbers. It's on the right-hand side of it. Can we go to the -- all right. I -- it may become relevant and it may not. That's -- that's yours -- Can -- Your Honours, can that be marked and admitted, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1451, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And, sir, I should have asked you this before. I think you were interviewed way back in 2005 by investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor, and the evidence that you're giving here today arises from what you told the investigators then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you a -- you had an opportunity to read through that interview yesterday, and are you satisfied that, with one exception, which we'll come to, what you said there you do not wish to alter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I was asking you about the split in the MUP. And I want you to have a look, please, at a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is 3 -- 65 ter 39 -- no, I'm sorry, it's already an exhibit. P650. And it's at tab 2C. And can we go, please, to the second page in both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of the events which are described here, which apparently took place in March, so before the formal separation of the two MUPs? And the incident described in this, effectively, complaint made by Muslim officers who had been removed from Pale and Sokolac Public Security Stations, in particular, that Malko Koroman, the chief, had informed the Muslim officers - and this is in the second paragraph - that there had been a decision by the Crisis Staff of Pale that all policemen of Muslim nationality must hand in their weapons and equipment. And he explained this was a counter-measure against the move made by the Stari Grad Public Security Station. So did you hear about this incident which involved the chief, Mr. Koroman, and the dismissal of the Muslim officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, next, about Mr. Koroman, who, it looks like, was also appointed on the 1st of April. And I needn't bother show you the document by Mico Stanisic. Had he been head before the split in the MUP of the SJB in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a career police officer, or had he done something else before being appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not a career police officer, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he appointed during the course of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the same day, we were received by the secretary of the city SUP. That's when I saw him for the first time. And on that day, we were both assigned to work in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had he done before he was appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What did you mean when you asked what he did before? Did you mean what his job was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Job. I did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a bank employee in Sarajevo. He has a degree in political sciences, where he majored with a defence studies or defence preparation studies, and I believe that in the bank he was in charge of putting things in place for the defence; something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do -- did you understand how he came to be appointed chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know how that transpired, but I suppose that he was delegated by the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you suppose that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because at the time, no appointment could be carried out without a -- the party blessing. For the same reason, I was seconded to Pale, because I was not a member of any of the parties, and there was no way for me to protect myself or defend myself from that move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Koroman was actually a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was before he joined the police. However, when he was a police employee, I know that he was an active member of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I don't know whether he was a member as such, but I know that he attended all the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to look, please, next, at a list of employees of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is 2 -- 65 ter 2126. And this is in April of 1992. Tab 5. Can we go into private session just for one question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That shows that in April of 1992 there were some 29 police -- sorry, 39, because they go over to the next page, members of the MUP in April. I want to ask you about some of them. First of all, could you tell us about Mr. Furtula, the deputy commander. What sort of police officer was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milomir is his name. Mr. Furtula was a good policeman, very conscientious, of high integrity, very well read, very literate, and that's why he remained working in the station. I don't know if he had any problems; he probably didn't because he was very good at what he did. If he hadn't been good, he would not have been kept on. He was good. He did everything that was necessary in terms of the paperwork, the administration. He was a true professional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Next, can I ask you about number 3, Jovan Skobo. Can you describe him, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovan Skobo was a traffic policeman in Sarajevo first, and then he was transferred to Pale. I didn't know him before I came to Pale myself. I can see here that at the time he was an assistant commander. Soon thereafter, perhaps in May, he was appointed commander. I'm not sure about the time-frame. I had a lot of negative experiences with that guy, Skobo. I didn't think much of him. I thought he was a bad man. That's as much as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any affiliation with any political party, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. However, judging from my experience, from the time that I spent there, I would say that he belonged to the circles moving around Mr. Krajisnik, that he was on very good terms with those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described him as a bad man. In what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know what? His attitude towards the Serbs was very arrogant. He was very arrogant too. He was not a professional in dealing with the Serbs. For example, in my case, and then in the case of a policeman whom he arrested, tied him against the radiator, and kept him there without any reason whatsoever. And he didn't even have the right to deprive him of his freedom. And he kept him there for three days. What else can one say about a man like that, if you know all those things? That person whom he arrested and he wanted to charge with some crimes or something, that policeman was never found guilty of any crimes, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of -- if I may of assistance. I don't think that his answer was properly recorded. So maybe he -- he should be asked to slowly repeat his answer because he explained this situation in more detail than is entered. Maybe it wasn't clear for the interpreters, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you speak reasonably slowly, because as you know it's being interpreted. You were describing that he was a very -- his attitude towards the Serbs was very arrogant. He was not a professional. And you described about a policeman who was arrested, tied to a radiator, although that doesn't appear on the transcript. That's what I heard you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there something else you wanted to add or did add about it? Mr. Zecevic thinks you said something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, no, actually. That will be all I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, I believe the witness -- because witness doesn't understand that his answer has not been recorded in the transcript. And probably that's why. He was saying about something that this person was taken in custody two times without proper foundation or something along these line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- sir, you describe that he arrested somebody who hadn't -- who was never charged with a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The man's name was Ivanovic; he was a policeman. And nobody was entitled to place an authorised official under arrest without the consent of the commander of the centre. That person was arrested twice. Nothing was every proven against him. No decision was ever issued to the effect of remanding him in custody. And after the second instance, after the second arrest, he lost his job without any explanation whatsoever. And -- I apologise, and another thing that I would like to say: I heard that vehicles belonging to non-Serbs that had been seized -- it took only the testimony of two witnesses to prove that those vehicles were his ownership, his property. Then he would sell those vehicles and -- and keep the proceeds, which all tells you about the character of that person, about the kind of man he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've mentioned non-Serbs and his selling of vehicles belonging to them. Were those non-Serbs who had left Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances. But there were also Serb vehicles that were parked in front of the Serb weekend cottages while their owners remained living in Sarajevo, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described him as effecting illegal arrest, tying people up to radiators. What his attitude towards the non-Serbs, the Muslims, in particular in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I never had an occasion to witness such instances. If any of those people came to the public station to discuss an issue or to report something, if non-Serbs arrived at the station to issue -- to discuss an issue and if they turned to the police, they did that in a different part. I wasn't there. I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you described Mr. Skobo being arrogant with Serbs. Did you never see him at any stage dealing with non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that at the public security station. I don't know if any -- anything of the kind happened while he was in the field. I did not have much dealings with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that non-Serbs came -- they came to the SJB, they would come to a different part. Do you mean a different part of the station from where you were based?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I'm afraid that that last answer needs to be redacted. It does rather ... from the public transcript. And can we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask that this list of the police station officials be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1452, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move, sir, to the question of -- we can see from that list, and, that's right, that by April of 1992, I think, there were no non-Serb police officers left in Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was just one woman. She was a Croat, and she worked in the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was she a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. My microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell her what the name -- tell her -- tell us what the name of this woman was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ana Simic. But she's not on the list that I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but we'll see her name if we go over the page in number 33 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anka. Yes, that's her. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move, now, please, to the question of the moving out from Pale of the non-Serb population. Could have you a look, please, at 2454.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is tab 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a list -- this is apparently a proposal made by the Muslim citizens of Pale. And the date, we can see, on the second page in each, English and in B/C/S, was the 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go back, then, to the first page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first proposal they wanted was that joint patrols be organised in predominantly Muslim populated settlements, composed of members of the Pale SJB and Muslim citizens. Did that happen? Were there joint patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, secondly: "That the public security service, on the territory of the Pale municipality, be carried out exclusively by members of the Pale SJB until the situation in the BH MUP is resolved." And [indiscernible] clear what that means, but were there other people patrolling Pale at that stage or taking part in -- in law-and-order activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to the fact that only Serb policemen had remained in the station at the time this document was drafted, it was only them who patrolled and protected people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were barricades removed in Pale? That's item number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember barricades. I know that there was some check-points at the exit from Pale, but that was 5 or 6 kilometres away. In Pale itself, I don't remember any barricades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It's -- but then number -- item number 10, says that: "Persons and families who do not feel safe on the territory of Pale municipality be allowed to leave the area without hindrance and in an organised manner."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go, please, over the page in -- we need to go over the page for that one. And then -- the bit that's added in brackets, over the page in both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason for that -- that request, made at number 10, is added in brackets: "(Due to reasons such as abuse, unlawful arrests of only Muslims, break-ins into apartments, disarming Muslim police officers, seizing personal weapons with permits, and similar)." Now, you've described about the -- or you've agreed that the description of the removal of the Muslim police officers happened. Were you aware that there were unlawful arrests taking place of Muslims and that apartments were being broken into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. And I wasn't aware of this request to leave and move to another place. I only saw it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for instances of breaking into the apartments, I don't know. But the weekend cottages of people who had their primary residence in Sarajevo, yes, I knew about that. I don't know, however, whether the perpetrators were police officers. Somebody broke into them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew that there were break-ins to the weekend cottages, but the perpetrators or the people who were breaking in were -- were unknown; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that they are unknown, but we could -- didn't have access to them because they lived in Sarajevo. So we mostly drafted Official Notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think there may have been a mistranslation there. You knew who owned the apartments, obviously. But are you saying that whoever broke into them were not identified, so that's why you say you can't say whether they were police officers or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last complaint is the seizing of personal weapons with permits and similar. By the 9th of April, had operations to disarm non-Serbs started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure it was then. There was disarming, but it seems to me that it was a bit later. Possibly it was at this time, however; I'm not sure. They were called upon to surrender their weapons, and I believe they did. I know that people were coming in to surrender their weapons, but I had nothing to do with that. It was done -- it was done by the police, but not me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, notwithstanding that he hadn't seen the document before, he is obviously familiar with the events, may I ask that it be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, very briefly, on the same topic at the next document, which is 2455, 65 ter 2455.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This looks like it's a response to that document issued by the -- the Muslims of Pale, the proposals made. And the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality came to the following conclusions: There is no reason for anybody to move out -- any Muslim to move out; the population will be -- continue to be supplied; and there should be an agreement. Now, can I first ask you this: First, had you ever seen this document before, and was it a public document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen this document, but I think that it was said publicly on television that people should not be afraid, that they could remained where they were. And I believe that that was the information broadcast on TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, God.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Zdravko Cvoro, who apparently was the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether Your Honours consider that -- that the fact that this was broadcast on -- on the radio or television would be sufficient. He hasn't seen the document before. But I would ask that it be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1454, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which conveniently brings us to the point that we would break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move now to the question of detention facilities in Pale. First of all, did you have facilities to detain prisoners within the SJB in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of 1992, were there prisoners kept in other facilities; and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later I found out that at the cinema house, which was close to the police station, some people were detained, although I don't know what the grounds for detention was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say later on you discovered this, how much later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found out about that when a suicide took place, when a barber from Korane, which is a settlement - I don't remember the man's name, but I knew him - when he committed suicide and when we were called to do an on-site investigation. On that occasion, I informed the investigating judge and the prosecutor. It was then that I found out that people were detained in the cinema house. I cannot remember precisely when this incident took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that -- well, first of all, who was guarding the facility at the cinema house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a while, I believed it was the Territorial Defence that was guarding that facility. Later on, I found out it was the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is one of the corrections that you made to what you originally said in interview. Who told you that it was, in fact, the police who were guarding this facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Furtula Milomir told me that. I asked him, because I believed it was the Territorial Defence guarding the facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he told you it was the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what sort of people were being detained there in -- in the cinema house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. But I believe that these were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you aware of any kind of ill-treatment that was taking place of the non-Serbs who were being detained in this cinema house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what was going on in there. I never went there. I simply don't or didn't know what was going on with the -- with the people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was responsible for making sure that people who were detained by police officers were being detained for proper, lawful reasons, and who were not being ill-treated whilst in detention in? Who was overall responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the chief of the public security station, Mr. Koroman, would be the person most responsible for such type of issues. However, if there was a need to detain anyone, then prior to that the person should be processed in order to determine whether there are grounds for detention. However, I didn't know anything about it. I was never informed by anyone how these people got detained, who detained them, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this, what you call the cinema house, the same as the Dom Kulture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I don't think that was Dom Kulture; that was a place where they were showing movies, earlier. It may have been Dom Kulture at some earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from that place, were you aware of any other facilities in which non-Serbs were being detained by the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally ever receive any complaints from non-Serbs whom you knew about either their places being robbed or their lawful weapons being taken or being, in any way, assaulted or ill-treated by police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one addressed me about that, so that I wouldn't know. Except that on several occasions I had a conversation with a friend of mine who used to work as a doctor in the -- in the health centre. Senaid Dubu [phoen] was his name. And on one occasion he complained, saying that he would have to go to Sarajevo. Prior to that, he had wanted to go to Serbia -- or, rather, Montenegro, because his wife -- or, rather, his wife's mother was originally from Montenegro. I tried to see whether I can arrange something for the departure of this man through Koroman, Malko, although the man didn't have any problems. He still worked at the time in the health centre. However, I didn't meet with any support -- or not that, it's -- it was impossible to do anything about it. He could go to Serbia using his normal ID; however, in the area around Zvornik, there were so-called Yellow Wasps who controlled a portion of the road. Not even the Serbs could pass though. Some of the ministers who tried to go there had problems as well. And on one occasion, as I way saying, this man complained, saying he has to go. And I asked him, How do you dare go to Sarajevo because your guys will kill you now if you're afraid to stay here? And he responded by saying, Well, if I don't leave with this group - because there was a group getting ready to go away - he said, If I don't go with this group, I will be killed before the next group leaves. He didn't tell me about any threats he received -- he had received, but I heard that after Serbian army had some casualties around Han Pijesak and members of the Serb army were from the Pale area, that after that a driver that worked for the health centre came in armed and forced him to get out of the building. That was, I think, in early June or around about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but there are a couple of interventions in the transcript. 41, line 8, I believe the witness said he still worked at the time in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In line 18, he -- I don't think it was recorded as -- as he said. But I don't want to mention it. Maybe you would consider that I suggest the answer to the witness. But please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this doctor said -- told you that he -- he was going have to leave with this group, because -- did he say to you, as is recorded: "If I don't go with this group, I will be killed before the next group leaves"? Or did he say something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What he said was the following: I -- I was afraid for his life, should he go to Sarajevo. And then he responded, If I don't go to Sarajevo now, if I go with the next group, then I'll be certainly killed. And he meant and I meant that he was afraid of the Muslims because he stayed working in the Serb-controlled area. And he was saying basically that he is not trusted either by the Serbs and will not be trusted by the Muslims but that he had to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying that -- that he wasn't afraid -- are you saying he wasn't afraid of what might happen to him from Serbs but was afraid of what might happen to him from the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That -- those were my fears in relation to him. But he said if he would not go with the first group, he would be in more trouble. If he would go with the second group, then the Muslims might detain him, even torture him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you, then, please, about something that you didn't know about. Could you have a look, please, in respect of prisoners, at a document which is already exhibited as P179.17.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 15A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a list of people - and you had a chance to look at it yesterday - of, as it's headed, a total of 400 persons who were driven from Bratunac to Pale. Do you remember 400 Muslim prisoners arriving from Bratunac in -- in the middle of Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw on one occasion, from the other side of the building where the cinema is located, it's a blind alley, and I saw a big truck that didn't have a tarpaulin on. In that truck, well, it was full of men. I think all of them had their hair cut really short. And that at one point someone told them that they are not supposed to look around, that they should bow their heads. It didn't last long. Very soon, they were driven towards the exit from Pale. I later found out they were sent for exchange. I've seen only one truck, and I don't know whether all these people could have been on that one truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person who told them that they're not supposed to look around and should bow their heads, was he is uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't anyone from the police. It was someone from the Territorial Defence who was there, because the Territorial Defence escorted them. They even had a vehicle of theirs, people from the Pale Territorial Defence. And they had their uniforms at the time, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was people from Pale, was it, who were with these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were escorting them, as far as I know, as far as I've seen. Now, whether there was anyone else - that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Next can I ask you, please, to have a look at the document - oh, dear - sorry. Can I just get this ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's the document 2459, 65 ter, and it's tab 19.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the Assembly, the Municipal Assembly, held on the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go to page 3 in English, and it's also the same in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a paragraph that begins: "Since the public security station was mentioned on several occasions during the discussion and many objections were raised about its work, Chief Malko Koroman asked for the floor."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's the top of the page in B/C/S, and it's the middle of the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "He informed the Assembly about the situation in the SJB. Four stations being formed. Three branches; the main one in Pale. And that a hundred men covered the central territory of Pale." And then he went on to say: "... as the operation in Renovica caused a lot of discontent due to the unjustified death of two men." Now, pausing there, sir, you described in some detail - and because of the limited time, I'm not asking you to go through that - that operation. Perhaps I could summarise it. Was this an operation that was conducted in order to disarm the non-Muslim -- the non-Serb population in Renovica which ran into resistance, and two police officers were killed during that operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's like this: These were non-Serbs, or Muslims, and their lawful weapons were supposed to be seized from them. And, then, in relation to that, allegedly, the chief, Malko Koroman, and the SDA president, Mr. Alija Prazina [phoen], made an arrangement --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to interrupt you. As I say, if anybody wants to ask you further details -- you've described the operation at length, but I'm more interested in what happened at the Assembly, I'm afraid. So is my summary correct, that you went on this operation, as you say, it was to disarm the Muslims, and in the course of that you ran into resistance and two police officers were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, here, at the Assembly, the -- Mr. Koroman is saying that -- or he was denying that: "The operation had been carried out at his initiative and claimed that the operation had been carried out in cooperation with the army command, which can be verified." Now are you able to confirm, because you were present during this operation, that there were members of the army present in the disarmament operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember if there was -- that there were any soldiers, apart from a couple of people from the Pale TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, do you know what happened to the village of Renovica after the two police officers had killed? If you don't, say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, on that day, that population withdrew. After we had been attacked, they withdrew toward Gorazde and Foca; those are Muslim-inhibited areas. And they withdrew in that direction. So some villages and hamlets surely were left unpopulated at the time, after withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any attack by armed forces, by Serb armed forces, on Renovica or any of the surrounding hamlets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know that the Serbs were attacking anybody at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Koroman, at the Assembly, then goes on to say this: "As far as the police going from Pale to Vrace in early May is concerned, the order for this operation came from the minister of the interior which is his right as defined by the Law on Internal Affairs." Can you explain what Mr. Koroman was talking about there? Explain briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in May. Maybe in early may or thereabouts, but I'm not sure. Anyway, a number of police officers was sent to Vrace. The street was called Ozrenska Street. And they were supposed to prevent Muslim units from taking the secondary school at Vrace, which was held by the Serbs. That was the MUP school. I know that there was some fighting there. I don't know if it was daily though. However, at that time, Mr. Jovan Skobo was wounded and that he was treated at the military medical academy in Belgrade, the VMA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was -- why was Mr. Koroman having to explain that it was the minister of the interior who had given that order? What was the complaint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I wasn't involved in these discussions. I didn't go -- I don't know when he went to those meetings. And we didn't have meetings at which he would brief us. I'm -- rarely saw him actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, on this, he -- he is asked by, obviously, a deputy to the Assembly why it was necessary to engage so many members of the MUP at Jahorina. And the chief replied that the number of men engaged in the area was not as large as claimed. That, in fact, there were 40 special police officers in an intervention group and 22 special police officers controlling the road at the place which is shown on the document - which I'm not going attempt to pronounce. Where did this special -- or this intervention group and special police officers, where did they came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose, since the government and all the ministries had their premises at Jahorina at the time, I suppose that these were people from the special unit who secured the ways there to fend off any possible attack or prevent any possible attack on those institutions at Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. What I'm asking is, did this intervention group, was that made up of officers from Pale, or was it a completely separate group of special police officers who came from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were police officers from Pale helping out. But I'm sure that they were police officers from the special unit. It isn't logical for a government to be put up in a mountainous area out of town and close to the demarcation line without such a unit being present. Whether there were police from Pale there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1455.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, could you have a look at the next document, dated the 19th of June, the day after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is document at tab 20; 2460.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a Municipal Assembly decision, as I say, the following day, but it arises from it, that session, saying that citizens of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity who wish to change their residence can exercise that right with the agreement of and permission of the Pale Public Security Station. "Changes of residence will be done in an organised manner, and the public security station is hereby put in charge of compiling a list of all persons wishing to change their place of residence, certifying the list in the Pale Municipal Assembly and compiling a list of all property owned by persons wishing to change their place of residence. And the public security station will guarantee safety of passage." Now, it may not have come directly within your competence, but were you aware of Muslims and Croats coming to the police station with a list of their goods and -- in order to move out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that, and I haven't seen this document before I came here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were wholly -- sorry. You were wholly unaware of this order by the President of the Pale Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, but it may have been exhibited in town as a flyer or a poster. But I don't remember seeing it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we can ask another witness to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal, please, with the problems that occurred at the Pale Police Station. And the simplest way of dealing with that is to look, please, at your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, can I ask that -- well, let's put up -- it's not put up on the screen for the public, and it's -- it is document - sorry, I just need to ... - number -- tab 48, and it's 317.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can we identify, sir, that's you're signature that we can see, as compiling this report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this report that you sent a truthful and accurate summary of what had been happening in the period of this report between the 1st of April and December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let go to the first -- sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go to the first page in English and in B/C/S -- or second page, rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It begins by saying that in that period which is covered in this: "The Pale Public Security Station investigation service operatives were engaged in many activities and tasks, which, by their nature, did not fall under their basic job title and scope of work." Can we pause there for a moment. What were those activities and tasks which didn't fall under their -- their -- normally under their title and scope of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let's say, murder. That didn't fall within our purview. And there were many murders at the time. People had to be detained, and we didn't have appropriate facilities. The prosecutor's office never got off the ground, so we had to feed the people, provide for their hygienic needs, et cetera. So that was one reason. But there were several reasons. I'm referring now to the first three months since the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may that be this will become clear when we go through your report. Paragraph 2: "In this period, the conditions of war and ... poorly organised activities at these levels resulted in the mass occurrence of all types of criminal activities committed by many people and the so-called war profiteers. "Due this, on this territory, we had many cases of motor vehicles stolen from other territories and driven around Pale. Their papers were arranged. Vehicles then taken to Serbia. A large number of forcible entries and robbing of weekend houses from which many things were stolen. Stealing of cattle." Now, it says "by" in the English translation, but I think in the Serbian it should be -- it says "from." Could you just read out, so we get the translation, from the words "the stealing of cattle." Could you read out what it says there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The stealing of cattle from persons of Muslim ethnicity who had fled into the forest or moved to Sarajevo, as well as other criminal offences."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. I think that was a matter when you were asked in interview about this. Then you go on to say: "All municipal departments and everybody else, especially the Pale Public Security Station and its management, were caught off guard by these phenomena. At the time, they did very little for the protection of property. They even participated in the execution of certain crimes because they thought, as they still do today, that they would never be held responsible for criminal activities." So are you referring there to employees, authorised employees, of Pale SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This certainly refers to a number of them, because it -- this couldn't all have happened without our involvement. The police was the most responsible for the protection of property such as weekend cottages, automobiles, and everything else. But, at the beginning, there were instances of all sorts of activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, continuing in the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we need to go into the third page in English. If we stay on the same page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you talk about refugees arriving, municipal authorities affected by bribery and corruption. And then about people being sent off to the houses that at this stage there was little the public security station could do to prevent it. And then you deal, in the next paragraph, with the personnel changes in the public security station and the deterioration in cooperation with police employees. Do you mean ordinary police employees and -- and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If carry on with this report, you then went on to give an overview of the actual crimes, which we can see on pages, in English, 4 and at the top of page 5. And, in the B/C/S, it's all set out on one page, which is the third page. And at the end of what I'm going ask you, I'm going to ask you to deal with the statistics in the log that are shown in the KU book, the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go, please, to the next page in English and to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You give the total of 64 criminal reports against 44 persons. 44 crimes committed by unknown perpetrators, of which 17 were solved at a later stage. "Due to the above mentioned reasons, police employees did not participate in the solving of the crimes. Taking into account the small number of people, negligence, idleness, and obstructions, it was objectively impossible to do anything more than that?" And then you go on to the criminal reports. Now, can we look at a specific incident you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's page 6 in English; and, in B/C/S, it's on the third page. Third page in B/C/S. Fourth page, sorry. My fault.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mention in the paragraph that begins: "During the report period, the criminal investigation service's operatives performed 66 on-site investigations ... and in the majority of cases, drafted reports or Official Notes. In two cases, however ... on the on-site investigation of forcible entry and theft, Mr. Dumovic failed to write a report and collect the photographic documentation for the murder of Muharem Kujovic and Koviljka Stankovic." Now, Mr. Kujovic, as you go on to talk about it, I think, there was a Muharem Kujovic and was his wife Hasna - we can see further on in the paragraph - also murdered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that they were married, that they were a couple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when we come to the book, we'll see there's no entry in the crime register for this incident. Is that because Mr. Hrsum - that should be -- I think, we saw his name earlier on the list: H-r-s-u-m, not N, as typed up - failed to write the appropriate report for the purposes of the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those cases, both an investigating judge and a prosecutor were part of the on-site investigation. A record was compiled and sent to the public security station. However, the officials at the crime department did not compile any official reports about those murders. No photos were taken. No pathology report was ever requested or compiled. So the file was never completed and was never sent to the Sokolac court. And that's why these cases were never recorded in the KU. They couldn't be recorded because they were never finalised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on in the next paragraph - and I'm not going to go through the whole thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But could we go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say: "Apart from the above mentioned, the criminal investigation service employees did not carry out any other work and failed to enter a ... number of events into the on-site investigation log-book." And you describe those. And you go on - and I don't propose to read out everything because it will take too long. But the next paragraphs, you describe the stealing of the Golf motor car ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go down, please, to the next page in English. At the bottom of the page in English. And I believe it is the next page in B/C/S as well. Top of the -- I'm not sure about that actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see, there, a paragraph that begins: "In the same vein, Tomo Hrsum interrogated several persons who participated in the crime of forcible entry ..." Does that appear there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "... and theft into a shop in Praca." Do you know whether that was -- was Praca an area that contained Muslim shops and houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that there were more Serbs than Muslims. There were Muslims, however. I'm not sure. I would say that the Serbs prevailed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this crime of forcible entry and there was a shop that was owned -- one by -- owned by Serbs or non-Serbs? If you don't, say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that there were more Serbs than Muslims residing in the Praca area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go, then, please, to the next page in English, the paragraph beginning: "In addition to this ..." Because you go on describing the various matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Having named all these police officers who were not performing their jobs, in addition to the above named individuals, probably completed some of their tasks but did not inform me of that. This was their usual practice (maybe even per somebody's instructions) ... these cases were never completed and forwarded to the competent services for further action. I always opposed such working methods, so I would tell them several times to finish a case. They would often take various items and things from the citizens, of which I was not informed ... they did it illegally because nothing was entered into the seized items log-book. On several occasions in their offices, I accidentally saw the seized items and immediately asked where they had come from ..." et cetera. And then you give more descriptions of that. Was that something -- this illegal seizure of property, was that something that was common or rare amongst the -- the officers in your station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a common occurrence, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we go, please, to the paragraph which at the next page in both the English and in B/C/S, beginning: "Also revealing is the example of Veljko Teletina ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a case where Mr. Teletina had been brought in, in connection with a murder of someone called Veselin Sarenac? What ethnicity was Veselin Sarenac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Koroman you actually approached, did you, to -- to help you bring in the person who was alleged to have committed the murder, Mr. Teletina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was after the murder. Things were not done properly immediately. People were afraid to go there because he was allegedly a dangerous person. And then I approached Koroman and asked him to do something about that, but nothing came out of that until the moment he was brought in during the night and then released again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you accused Mr. Koroman, there, of abusing his official authority and, indeed, extending help to an officially prosecuted perpetrator of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page in English, and I believe -- I'm trying -- sorry I'm just trying to find the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see on the page there: "Negligence and idleness started at this beginning of 1992 ..." Do you see that paragraph? Is that on that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is page 6, if I may -- if I can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic. Can we go to page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 7 of the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, 7. All right. Yup.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say: "I warned Malko Koroman about that on several occasions, asking to tell the people not to behave like that, because I knew they were under his influence, that he spent all his time at work and outside of work with them. Since he never did anything in June, I informed Koroman in writing, asking him to take steps in order to prevent Mr. Kovac, Mr. Hrsum from continually being absent, et cetera, to warn them about idleness and negligence and impossible to working on -- that it was impossible to go on working with people in that manner. And I warned Koroman that if he did not take any steps, I would inform the MUP, but he told me not to do that." Was that an accurate description of -- of what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then a couple more paragraphs in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go to page 13 in English. And it's page -- the ninth page in the B/C/S, I believe. Ninth page; is that it? No -- yeah. Just a moment. Just let me check that. Is there a -- is there -- yes. I believe it's -- it's on that page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a paragraph that begins: "On the 6th of April, 1992, the criminal investigation service employees took 18 carpets from a group of people travelling from Istanbul to Sarajevo. Mr. Koroman gave four carpets, together with Mr. Juvicic, that gave four carpets to Romanijaprevoz." And then you go on: "However, just before I wrote this report, I found out that Koroman and Skobo divided the kilims amongst themselves." Then you talk in the next paragraph about weapons, and you allege that Malko Koroman distributed the seized weapons to a certain number of people from the service and outside of it. Again, was that, as you understood it, a truthful and accurate description of what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again, if I can be of assistance. I don't think that's the right page, from what you were reading. It's page 8 of the transcript in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought I had marked it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That begins: "On the 6th of April ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. Yes, now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. Were those two paragraphs that you put there accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally, on this report, please, can we go to page 16 in English; and tenth page, I hope, in B/C/S. I hope that's right. Perhaps Mr. Zecevic can help me. I thought I had this marked properly. Does that show the paragraph: "In addition to the above and in spite of having been informed of this ..."? "In addition to the above and in spite of having been informed of this," does that appear on that page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps can you help. "Have you ever done anything in order to establish Jovan Skobo's disciplinary and criminal responsibility?" Is that on that page? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see it in front of me. Oh -- at the beginning? The thing at the beginning, perhaps? No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry, I believe it's page 11. That's the very last paragraph of the document? Is that what you're reading?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No, it's not the last paragraph of the document. I'm reading -- if you look at the English, Mr. Zecevic, you will see: "In addition to the --" it comes after the last long equally -- side of the paragraph. It should -- I thought it was on the top, the second paragraph in B/C/S, at the top of page 3588589. Does that begin: "In addition to the above and in spite of having been informed of all this ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I found it Ms. Korner. It's page 10 of the Serbian version. In e-court, the second paragraph. Page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't see how that can be -- unless there's a very -- a complete difference between the English and the -- yes. That's the bit. Well, that's the bit I was looking at. So why are we doing that? It was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Do you see that paragraph, sir, after all of that faffing around the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only references to Skobo in front of me is with regard to blank drivers licences, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does the next paragraph start: "Other organs were sent 86 regular mail items"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the paragraph before that not say, in the Serbian language: "In addition to the above and in spite of having been informed of this ..." you're going -- you've gotten -- you've given a long list of Skobo's misdemeanours "... neither the CSB nor the MUP have ever done anything in order to establish Jovan Skobo's disciplinary and criminal responsibility."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The paragraph that follows says: "Other organs were sent 86 regular mail items, and the CSB was sent eight Official Notes, one on-site investigation report, one written statement about the circumstances of war crimes and genocide against the Serbian population ..." Had there been a request for investigation into potential war crimes and genocide against the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I used the word "genocide." The word was misplaced because you have to believe me when I tell you that we didn't know what genocide was until recently. But that word did come up in various conversations. What I meant -- what I had in mind were murders, war crimes, but you certainly cannot talk about genocide, can you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry about -- yes. Don't worry about the technical legal definition of genocide. But what I want to know is: You specifically mentioned that. Had there been a request that you provide information to the CSB about any war crimes, whether called war crimes or genocide, against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We submitted all our investigation materials, all documents which concerned war crimes, but not only in reference to Serbs but also to other ethnic group. We followed a regular procedure in that respect. But when it came to war crimes, I believe there was a request for those to be well-documented, accompanied by photos ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point is, sir, what you don't mention in this report, war crimes, generally, against whoever, you specifically mention war crimes, leave out genocide, against the Serbian population. And I'm asking you if you can recall whether had you been specifically requested by the CSB in respect of war crimes committed against the Serbian population. If you can't remember whether that was a specific request, then say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. This here applies to some of the villages in the direction of Gorazde, on the border with Pale. Those were Serb hamlets, hamlets inhabited by Serbs. And I remember that in that part a grandfather was killed, together with his 13-year-old grandson. That grandson had his ears, nose, and three fingers on the right hand cut off. There was somebody else there. His mother was also killed, I think. And I believe that that this refers to that incident. But this also applies -- or at least some of it applies to the village of Sainovic, in the same area where some Serbs had been killed, some of them by rifles and others were slaughtered just like in the first case, because that young boy was -- had his throat slit. Those are the cases that are described herein.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the last time, I understand that. But were you being specifically requested by the CSB to give them information - that's the question - otherwise why is it -- there's no mention of war crimes committed against Muslims or, indeed, Croats for that mention -- for that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember whether that was an express request. But I know that those documents were being collected, all those photos were being put together. I don't know why. I suppose that it was some -- to serve some future needs, the purposes of some future trial, should it ever take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, sir. That's all that I ask about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may it be admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1456, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's as far as we can go for today. Mr. Witness, we're about to take the adjournment for today. And I'm obliged to point out to you that, having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with the lawyers from either side until you are released by the Chamber. And should you have any conversations with anybody outside the courtroom, you can't discuss your testimony before the Chamber. So we adjourn, to reconvene in this courtroom, tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
